## Stereo Baited Remote Underwater Video

Fish communities can be characterized by characteristics such as their
species compositions, abundances, and length structures [(Babcock et al.
(1999)](https://doi.org/10.3354/meps189125). Underwater video
observations can help us obtain these characteristics [(Schmid et al.
2024)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-70636-8). Underwater video
observations are a low-impact sampling technique that are particularly
useful in observing fish in hard-to-reach areas, deep and dangerous
waters inaccessible to divers, and at night [(Lowry et al.
2012)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jembe.2012.01.013). If we want to
collect data on marine organisms in their natural behavior without
attracting them with bait, we can use unbaited cameras. These unbaited
cameras are best for studying the behavior of fish and other organisms
in their natural state, assessing the biodiversity and community
structure of marine habitats without the influence of bait, and
monitoring habitat use and interactions among species that might be
disrupted by the presence of bait [(Harvey et al.
2007)](https://doi.org/10.3354/meps07192).

A baited remote underwater videocamera (BRUV) can help in assessing the
presence and abundance of elusive species such as sharks and other
predators, and for conducting fish population surveys, especially in
areas with low visibility. The bait lures these predators, that would
otherwise not be seen, to the camera. Usually fish meat from oily fish
is used as bait, and this is placed in front of the camera.

```{r, echo=FALSE,out.width="49%", out.height="20%",fig.cap="*Left: A BRUV on the sea floor. the BRUV has only a single camera. The bait is placed in front of the camera attracting large (piscivorous) fish. Image courtesy of AIMS. Right: Inspection of a stereo BRUV by divers. The two cameras of the stereo BRUV can clearly be seen*", fig.show='hold',fig.align='left'}
knitr::include_graphics(c("BRUV_aims.jpg","Stereo_BRUV2.jpg"))
```

BRUVs generally consist of a steel or aluminium frame, with cameras
inside. This frame is lowered to the sea floor, and the cameras shoot
images for about one hour. After this hour, the frame and cameras are
retrieved and the footage stored and analyzed.

In order to estimate abundance from video footage, *MaxN* (Maximum
Number of Individuals) is a metric commonly used in underwater video
analysis. *MaxN* refers to the highest number of individual organisms of
a particular species observed in a single video frame during the
recording period [(Campbell et al.
2015)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fishres.2015.05.011). It effectively
accounts for the peak abundance of that species at one time. While
*MaxN* is a useful metric, it may not provide an exact estimation of
total abundance due to potential variations in fish behavior, movement,
and attraction to bait. However, it is generally considered a useful
metric for comparing differences among habitats, or trends over time.
Other metrics for relative abundance information include the time until
the first observation of a species.

If the (B)RUV is equipped with two cameras, we can use stereo vision to
estimate the distance of objects relative to the camera in three
dimensions, and hence also the size of objects [(Langlois et al.
2020)](https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13470).
This is what we will be doing in this practical. We will try to estimate
the size of objects without disturbing them (just like we would do with
the fish in our communities).

We do not need to go too deep into the theory of how to stereo cameras
allow estimating distances in three dimensions, but it uses **Direct
Linear Transformation** (DLT; [Abdel-Aziz and Karara
(1971)](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/5dba/c464792ba6dccaff073a46e42470151c449b.pdf)).
In stereo-vision or 3D reconstruction, this is the method used to
compute 3D coordinates of points from their 2D projections in multiple
camera views. DLT requires camera calibration: we need known 3D points
and their 2D projections to determine a projection matrix. This
calibration is based on having objects of known dimensions in a set of
stereo-video frames. The more views and better calibration, the more
accurate the 3D reconstruction.

## SBRUV software

In order to operate the stereo vision for a BRUV, we first need to
calibrate the stereo-cameras before we can analyze the video footage. We
will be using the R package `SBRUV` to first calibrate the cameras and
then take some measurements with the SBRUV.

## The checkerboard

Camera calibration in StereoMorph is based on a checkerboard pattern
(Olsen 2017): The internal corners in the checkerboard provide points in
a plane that can easily be detected automatically. **For calibration,
several frames must be captured with the checkerboard in different
positions and orientations, by both cameras simultaneously** .

The checkerboards have a number of internal corners along the x
(horizontal) and y (vertical) dimensions. Note that the number of
internal corners are not the number of squares but the number of
intersections of black squares. **Our checkerboards have 8 internal
corners and 6 internal vertical corners.**

We also need to know the "square size”. This refers to the length along
any one side of the square. Our checkerboards are exactly square, so
measuring the length of one side should be enough. **Our checkerboards
square size is 3.04 cm**.

```{r, echo=FALSE,out.width="49%", out.height="20%",fig.cap="*Left: A checkerboard with counts of horizontal and vertical corners in red, and the definition of the square size in blue. Right: Schematic illustration of stereo vision using Direct Linear Transformation*", fig.show='hold',fig.align='left'}
knitr::include_graphics(c("20250410_120201_4.jpg","Screenshot stereocameras.png"))
```

## Shooting video for calibrating the SBRUV

Our SBRUVs use two GoPros. They are named after the number of the BRUV,
and "left" and "right". Each SBRUV has a GoPro remote that connects to
two cameras simultaneously. This allows starting the videos on both
cameras at the same time.

To use the two GoPros in the SBRUVs, turn on the GoPRos using the power
button on the side of the GoPro. Once both cameras are on, turn on the
remote. the screen of the remote should now say "Connect to", with the
option "Multicam". Select the muticam option by pressing on the front
button (with the big red square). Once the button is pressed, and both
cameras connected, the remote should say "Ready, 2 Cameras".

The GoPros show the operating mode in the front screen. First, we can
see if the camera is in "time lapse", "video" or "photo" mode. *Make
sure it is in "Video mode"*. If the GoPros are not yet in video mode,
this mode can be selected using the "mode" button on the GoPro remote.


For the calibration, we need to have ninety seconds of footage of the
checkerboard, at different locations in both camera views, and from
different distances. Make sure to have video of the checkerboard pattern
being moved and rotated throughout the entire calibration space.

![](Screenshot_calibration.png)

Use the remote to start recording on both cameras, by pressing the front
button. In the one-minute video that you record, move the checkerboard
through the field of view of both cameras. **Move slowly**. Try to get
some footage of the checkerboard near the camera, and some further away.

## Shooting video for our observations

Now that we have the footage for calibration, we can film objects and
**use the stereo footage to estimate the position of points visible in
both images to in 3 dimensions**. This is called "digitizing" the
observations, and the points that we want to digitize are called
"landmarks". Once we know the positions of landmarks in three dimensions
we can estimate distances between these landmarks.

Try to film a few objects using the stereo cameras, using the same
procedure that was used for the calibration: turn on both cameras, and
start recording on both cameras using the remote in "multicam" mode. In
this practical, we will shoot one minute of video in the "Custom"
profile. When making observations in the filed, you will set the camera
to shoot longer videos.

## Getting the footage from the GoPros

Getting the footage from the two cameras requires opening the side of
the GoPros and connecting them by USB to a computer. We filmed the
footage for calibration and observation before handling the cameras so
that we made sure **the angle between the cameras did not change between
calibration and observations.** 

Copy the calibration footage from the two GoPros to the `calibration` directory that you created earlier. Make
sure to copy the videos into a single folder, and to **name the video
from the left camera "left.mp4", and from the right camera
"right.mp4"**. This consistent naming is needed to be able to link the
calibration videos with the observations.

Next, store the observation footage in the `observations` directory that
we created earlier. **Make sure to name the video file from the left
camera "left.mp4", and from the right camera "right.mp4"**. This is
needed so that the digitizing app knows how to link the images to the
calibration. Ultimately, the directory structure should look something like the structure below.

* SBRUV (as example of working directory)
  + calibration
    - left.mp4
    - right.mp4
  + observations
    - left.mp4
    - right.mp4
 

## Calibrating the cameras

Now we calibrate the cameras. This is done using the
`calibrateCameras()` function. This function tries to detect the
checkerboard in both left and right calibration video files. Your videos
will need to be synchronized in order for the calibration to work
properly (the first frame in all views must correspond to the same point
in time). Because we started the videos at the same time and used the
same frame rate, they should be synchronized.

```{r eval = F}
# Call to the calibrateCameras() function, the settings for inner corners and square size are
# already filled in. In this 
calibrateCameras(img.dir = cal_dir,             # name of the calibration directory
                 nx = 8,                        # number of horizontal inner corners 
                 ny = 6,                        # number of vertical inner corners  
                 sq.size = "3.04 cm",           # square size
                 cal.file = 'calibration.txt',  # name of the calibration file
                 undistort = TRUE, num.aspects.read = 50, 
                 fit.min.break = 2, nlm.calls.max = 15,
                 objective.min = 0.8, num.sample.est = 20,
                 num.aspects.sample = 4, num.sample.sets = 3, objective.min.break = 1.2)
```

In this code `nx` is the number of horizontal inner corners, `ny` is the
number of vertical inner corners, and `sq.size` is the size of the
square. The size of the square has to be provided within quotation
marks, and include the units of the measurement, e.g. '64.43 mm', or
'12.43 cm'. Remember that in our case this is "3.025 cm".

The `cal.file` argument takes the name of the calibration file written
to disk. We need this calibration file when digitizing observations. The
`num.aspects.read` argument gives the number of frames being analyzed
for checker board corners. Most other parameters deal with the amount of
computation going into the calibration. Leave them as they are for now.

The `calibrateCameras()` function will begin by trying to detect the
corners in all of the calibration images. The frames with detected
corners are stored in the “Verify” folder. **The calculations behind the
calibration takes approximately 5 minutes**.

Only those corners simultaneously detected in both views can be used to
estimate calibration coefficients. The number of cases for which corners
are detected in at least 2 views is printed in the output. For this
tutorial, having more than 5 cases with corners detected in both views will suffice.

After the checkerboard corners have been detected and undistortion
coefficients estimated, the function estimates DLT calibration
coefficients. Once calibration is done, `calibrateCameras()` prints a
“dltTestCalibration Summary”. 

-   Aligned ideal to reconstructed (AITR) errors: The AITR error aligns
    an ideal (perfect) checkerboard to the reconstructed corners. Then,
    the distance between each ideal checkerboard corner and its
    corresponding reconstructed corner is measured. If the corners were
    perfectly reconstructed, the ideal and reconstructed points would
    overlap perfectly. The “AITR RMS errors” are the alignment errors
    along each dimension (x,y,z) in the coordinate system of the
    calibration points. This coordinate system depends on the
    orientation of the first checkerboard so it is somewhat arbitrary.

## Making and digitizing observations

Now that the cameras are calibrated and DLT parameters obtained, we
**use our observations stereo footage to estimate position of points in
3 dimensions**. This is called "digitizing" the observations, and the
points that we digitize are called "landmarks". Once positions of
landmarks in three dimensions are known we estimate distances between
landmarks.

The first thing we do is to split the video in separate frames using the
`extractFramesDir()` function, which takes the observations directory as
argument. The 'nth' argument allows extracting every *n^th^* frame only,
to reduce the number of extracted frames. The default value for 'nth' is
1, so that all frames are extracted. Setting it to 24 would extract a
single frame for every second of video (because video fps is 24).
This function extracts all frames from the video into a sub-directory
named "images" within the observations directory. In order to digitize
the images, we also need the calibration file that we made earlier. This
calibration file contains the DLT parameters. We also copy the calibration
text file to the observations directory using the `file.copy()` function
in R. This takes a file name to copy (in this case our
calibration_gopro.txt file), and copies it to another location (in this
case it creates a copy named calibration_gopro.txt in the observations
directory).

```{r eval = F}
extractFramesDir(img.dir = obs_dir, nth = 1)
file.copy("calibration.txt" , file.path(obs_dir,"calibration.txt"))
```

Now that we have the calibration file for the DLT parameters, our stereo
observations, and the landmarks that we want to digitize, we can digitize the images, using the `digitizeImages()` function.

```{r eval = F }
digitizeImages(image.file = file.path(obs_dir, 'Images'), 
               shapes.file = file.path(obs_dir, 'Shapes 2D'),
               landmarks.ref = c("snout","caudal_fin"), 
               cal.file = file.path(obs_dir,'calibration_gopro.txt'))
```

Running this command will open the digitizing part of StereoMorph. Here,
we have to indicate where the landmarks are in both views of a single
frame. The example below is for digitizing several landmarks on oceanic
whitetip shark (*Carcharhinus longimanus*). In our example for fish
lengths we have only two landmarks. In the right-bottom corner of the
digitizing part of StereoMorph we see the frame number and the camera
view (left or right).

The buttons above the views and frames allow switching between them. Alternatively you can switch between frames using the "," and "." keys on your keyboard. To get a 3D location of a landmark in a frame, we need to have the position
of the landmark in both 2D frames in the video. Make sure you indicate
2D positions in both views for at least 4 frames if you want to get a
reliable estimate of the distances between landmarks in 3D.

There is a 'settings' tab in the digitizing app. One of these settings is to show the epipolar line. The epipolar line is the line in one image that corresponds to a point in the other image, along which the matching point must lie (according to epipolar geometry). This arises because each 3D point is seen from two cameras, and the geometry between them restricts where matches can appear. The epipolar line is shown in an image when a landmark is selected in the other view. The epipolar line can help find correct landmark matches, for instance to identify the corresponding fish in two views. 

![](Screenshot_digitizing.png)

Once you have digitized at least 4 frames, we can reconstruct the 3D
locations, and put them into the R workspace as shapes. This is done
using the `reconstructStereoSets()` function.

```{r eval = F}
shapes <- reconstructStereoSets(shapes.2d = file.path(obs_dir, 'Shapes 2D'), 
                      shapes.3d = file.path(obs_dir, 'Shapes 3D'),
                      cal.file  = file.path(obs_dir, 'calibration.txt'))

```

Now that we have the 3D shapes, with the 3D positions of the landmarks,
we can estimate the distances between the landmarks, in this case
between the snout and the caudal fin, being the length of the
fish. As you see, we get as many estimates of this length as the
number of frames that we digitized. The R code below calculates distances between snout and caudal fin, and applies this for all frames. Ultimately, this yields the distance between snout and caudal fin for all fish that we have digitized, and prints these distance by frame.

```{r eval = F}
distances(shapes)
```

## Answer the following questions

If you know the true size of the objects, could you
estimate the bias in the measurements? Finally, can the distances of the
object that you measured somehow be retrieved from the outputs? Or their
speeds?

## Wrapping up

We have now shown how to repeated measure length for a single
fish/object from a one minute video. In the field, we would like to know
more about the size composition of the community. \* How would we design
a setup that allows estimating size composition, while making sure we
avoid pseudo-replication. \* Could we estimate fish abundance and
density from the footage? \* We may also be interested in the distance
of a fish school from the BRUV: If we do not bait it so that fish show
their normal behaviour and we place it facing up, we could then estimate
the height of the fish above the sea floor.

Using these kinds of estimates we are able to answer hypotheses about
the ecology of fish in a low-impact manner and SBRUVs have proven to be
a reliable tool for doing so. Much of the modern research on sharks and
other predators on reefs are done with the help of SBRUVs.

**As a final note, please make sure of the following if you want to use
a SBRUV in the field:**

-   Make sure that you bring the remote that is paired with the GoPros
    in the BRUV.

-   The GoPros should always be in their underwater housing when
    deployed. Make sure you close the underwater housing properly and
    regularly check the seals of the housing

-   Make sure all equipment that has been in contact with seawater gets
    rinsed with freshwater after use. Given the limited battery life of
    the GoPros, make sure to charge them at the end of the day so they
    are ready for use the next morning.

-   Remember that the calibration needs to be redone if the position or
    angles of the cameras with respect to each other changes. Make sure
    these remain fixed, and calibrate the camera regularly.

-   Make a checklist for yourself before lowering the SBRUV. This
    checklist should include things like:

    -   Is the line attached to the buoy properly attached and running
        free?
    -   Does the depth not exceed the length of the line attached to the
        BRUV?
    -   Are the batteries charged?
    -   Is there enough space on the SD cards left?
    -   Are the right presets selected on both GoPros?
    -   Are both GoPros recording when being lowered?
